The second concerns knowledge and power.

As we have seen, the Muʿtazilites understood these attributes, like all the other divine attributes, as identical with God’s own essence. Since God’s essence is infinite and encompasses all beings without exception, his knowledge and power must also be infinite and must include everything that exists.
From this, the Muʿtazilites concluded that created beings themselves must be finite.
If they were infinite, this would mean, first, that they too were eternal—and nothing is eternal except God, who created them.
Second, it would mean that God’s knowledge and power did not fully encompass them, because one infinite thing cannot completely encompass another infinite thing.
These were basic starting points for Muʿtazilite thinkers and, later, for the Ashʿarites as well. At their root, they came directly from Islamic belief.

The earliest Muslims, and especially the traditionalists who followed the teachings of the early generations, accepted these principles simply as matters of faith required by the religious texts. They did not think rational or theoretical proofs were needed. In fact, they resisted attempts to provide such proofs.

But from the ninth century onward, Arab-Islamic culture entered a period of intense intellectual development. Thinkers could no longer be satisfied with statements of faith alone. They increasingly felt the need to give those beliefs a theoretical foundation.
For the material needed to build that foundation, they turned to the body of philosophical knowledge reaching them from the different intellectual sources available in their society and their time.
This was the setting in which the new rational schools arose, above all the Muʿtazila.

They examined each new philosophical idea and asked whether it contained something that could be absorbed, transformed, and made into part of the theoretical foundation for one of their religious or doctrinal positions.
Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf was the first Islamic thinker—not merely the first Muʿtazilite—to find in atomism, or the theory of the individual substance, a theoretical basis for several key beliefs.
The theory had reached Muslim thinkers from ancient Indian and Greek philosophy.

Al-ʿAllāf used it to support the belief that God alone is eternal while the world came into existence; to explain how God’s infinite knowledge and power encompass all finite individual things; and to explain the relationship between God and the world.
So what exactly was this atomic theory?
In its Greek form, atomism goes back to its first founder, Leucippus, and to Democritus, who developed it further.
Democritus developed the theory at a time when the ideas of the Eleatic philosophers, especially Zeno, were influential.

The Eleatics denied that motion really existed. They even denied that motion could be thought about consistently. Zeno believed that existence involved contradictions, and that sensory knowledge and rational knowledge stood in conflict with one another.

Leucippus, Democritus, and Anaxagoras therefore opposed the Eleatic teachings. They developed theories meant to show that motion does exist in the natural world and that sensory and rational knowledge do not necessarily contradict one another.

These thinkers assumed that there were infinitely many material particles. But they also assumed that empty space existed, and that the particles moved through this void eternally, without beginning or end.
In one surviving passage from his works, Democritus presents the theory through three basic ideas: the principles of the universe, the atoms, and the void.
“Atoms” was the name that Democritus and his teacher Leucippus gave to these particles. The Greek word atom means something that cannot be divided.

Leucippus and Democritus believed that these particles were infinite in number and could not be divided. This is why their theory became known as the doctrine of the “indivisible part,” or the “individual substance.”
Their atoms therefore had three basic features.
First, they were infinite in number.
Third, they were completely solid: there was no empty space inside them.
Democritus also held that atoms had so many different outward forms that they could not be counted or fully grasped by the mind.
Atoms differed from one another in shape, size, position, and arrangement.
They could also interact in different ways. Sometimes they met and became intertwined. At other times they repelled one another and moved apart.
Their shapes varied. Some were spherical, others rounded, others pyramid-shaped, and so on.
They also varied in size, from small to smaller and smaller still, until they reached a size too small to be seen.

They differed in position as well. Democritus illustrated this through the numerals 6 and 2: if the orientation of the numeral 6 is reversed, changing the direction of the angle it forms from left to right, it becomes 2. The reverse is also true. The same idea can be illustrated by reversing the direction of the Arabic letter ʿayn.
Atoms also differed in arrangement, rather as the position of the Arabic letter bāʾ differs in the words ab and bāʾ.
For Democritus, the way atoms sometimes join together and sometimes move apart explains how bodies are formed in the natural, material world.

“Atoms are basically small bodies with no particular quality. The void is the space in which they move eternally, from above to below. As they move, they either become intertwined in one way or another, or they collide and push one another apart. They separate, then come together again in new combinations. In this way they produce other complex bodies, including our own bodies, together with their states and sensations.”
Other statements by Democritus tell us that as atoms move, they meet and combine to form a particular body. They remain in that arrangement for a certain period, then separate again.
How long a particular combination lasts depends on how long the body formed by those atoms continues to exist, or how long the larger unit formed by those particles remains together.
Another statement gives us a clearer picture:

“The atoms move rapidly through infinite empty space, where there is no above or below, no middle, no end, and no boundary. They move through this space in such a way that collisions cause them to hold together. From this arise everything that exists and everything that can be sensed.”
4 — The Atomic Explanation of the Material World
From this account of Democritus’s atomism, we can see that the phenomena of the natural world are explained through atomic combinations.
If matter is analyzed far enough, it eventually resolves into an infinite number of atoms moving eternally through an infinite void.
One conclusion follows directly from this: motion is the natural state of matter.
This was the opposite of what the Eleatics, and especially Zeno, had argued.
Both ancient and modern accounts of Democritus often describe the atoms themselves as being, while the void is described as non-being.
But for Democritus this does not mean that the void is somehow less real than the atoms.
Rather, atoms and void form a kind of unity of opposites.
The Eleatic philosophers had reasoned about motion in the following way:
There can be no motion without empty space. But empty space does not exist. Therefore motion does not exist.
He accepted the first statement: there can be no motion without empty space.
But he began from a different basic assumption—the fact that motion exists.
If motion really exists, then empty space must exist as well.
Democritus also included in his atomism the idea that being itself does not change.
He took this idea from the Eleatic philosophers. It stands in contrast to Heraclitus’s view that things continually arise and disappear through a process of becoming.
Democritus believed that the existence of many different things did not contradict the unity of being. For him, there could be no multiplicity without unity.

When Aristotle explained the atomism of Leucippus and Democritus in his Metaphysics, he said that they accepted both the full and the empty—being and non-being—as the two basic elements from which reality is composed.
According to Aristotle, this meant that for Leucippus and Democritus, being was no more real than non-being, just as solid body was no more real than empty space.
These, Aristotle said, were the purely material causes of existing things.
Some philosophers recognized only one basic substance from which everything was made. They explained the different phenomena of the world as different changes in that one substance.
Leucippus and Democritus did something similar. They took fullness and emptiness as the two basic principles and explained all other phenomena through changes in the atoms.
But they reduced the differences between atoms themselves to three things: shape, position, and arrangement.
To complete our account of the different sides of atomism, we should also note Democritus’s insistence that motion cannot be separated from matter.
For him, the motion of atoms had no beginning.
In this sense, he was explaining nature through nature itself.
Through this theory, Democritus became the first thinker in the history of Greek science to raise the problem of space and time in this form.
Space was the vast void through which atoms had moved from eternity.
Time was contained in the very idea of motion.
Democritus also believed that empty space existed inside bodies, allowing them to contract and expand.
He regarded space as discontinuous. At the same time, he denied that it could be divided physically and practically into an infinite number of parts.
This did not mean that infinite division was impossible in geometry or mathematical operations, where the process could be repeated endlessly through an unlimited series of hypothetical divisions.
Here Democritus’s mathematical view of infinity met his atomic theory.
Democritus’s advanced theories provoked the hostility of the Greek aristocracy, whose outlook found expression in Plato’s idealism. Plato himself came from the highest ranks of the nobility.
From Plato onward, idealist thinkers tried to distort Democritus’s theory and reduce its importance in the history of philosophy.
Yet the importance of Democritus’s view of the universe can also be seen in the way it explained generation and destruction—the coming into existence and passing away of things.
His account of the universe, based on the atomic structure of matter, contains a rich element of spontaneous dialectical thinking.
For Democritus, the motion of atoms through the vast void explains how worlds arise and disappear.
And there is not just one world. The universe contains an immeasurable number of worlds.
An infinite number of atoms move eternally through infinite space. In different parts of that space, they gather into whirlpools. Through their motion and gathering, different worlds are formed.
As groups of atoms swirl together, they collide sideways. This produces an outer shell that separates the newly forming world from the other parts of the universe.
Epicurus (341–270 BCE) agreed with Democritus that nothing exists except atoms and the void.
Everything else, including all the phenomena of nature, consists of different combinations of atoms.
The appearance and disappearance of any particular thing is simply the result of atoms coming together or moving apart.
Nothing comes from nothing, and nothing becomes nothing.
Epicurus explained the point in this way.
Nothing can arise from something that does not exist. If it could, then anything could arise from anything else, without any need for seeds or beginnings.
The reverse is also true. If things that disappear simply ceased to exist altogether—if they became nothing—then everything would have vanished long ago.
The universe would then have remained forever without change, because there would be nothing for it to turn into, and nothing outside the universe that could enter it and cause change.
Although Epicurus took many ideas from Democritus, especially the idea that all things and events are governed by causal necessity, he also introduced a number of new ideas.
In doing so, he tried to overcome some of the historical limits of Democritus’s atomism.
Democritus had not solved the problem of the weight of atoms, and he had restricted their movement to a straight line.
This gave his atomism a somewhat deterministic character.
Epicurus therefore insisted that atoms have weight.
